Recent work supports text-informed sequential recommendation, but the retrieved papers do not establish the exact combination of BERT4Rec, lightweight title/description encoding trained entirely from scratch, and fine-grained intent learning. [ITS-Rec (2025)](https://www.mdpi.com/2079-9292/14/9/1748) uses BERT-derived representations of titles, descriptions and reviews; its results therefore do not directly establish feasibility under the present data and initialization constraints. [H-BERT4Rec (2024)](https://aaltodoc.aalto.fi/items/c0a7956b-4358-4429-8d46-282e1d864f8f) enriches BERT4Rec with pretrained heterogeneous-network embeddings, another materially different setting. The [2024 MMSR empirical study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.17372) examines content encoders, fusion and sequential architectures, but its abstract’s “from scratch” framework construction should not be interpreted as proof that all text encoders use random initialization.

A constraint-compatible research hypothesis is a small, randomly initialized token embedding layer with mean pooling or a shallow CNN over available titles/descriptions, projected and gated into item-ID representations inside one jointly trained BERT4Rec network. Train the text encoder through masked-item prediction and use the same composite item representations for candidate scoring. This is a proposed experiment, not a demonstrated result from the retrieved literature. Preserve [BERT4Rec’s Cloze objective](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.06690): hide both the target ID and its text at masked input positions, then append a mask for inference. Compare against the corrected ID-only baseline using fixed macro validation HR@10; inspect sparse-item behavior and overly broad textual similarity before attributing improvements to fine-grained intent.
